title: Second Verse
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Greg had written a second verse on the back of a receipt.

The first verse filled nearly a page of his notebook. The second consisted of three crossed-out words, a coffee stain, and a drawing of what might have been a sad guitar. I studied it while he adjusted the recording levels.

"Powerful," I said.

"It's a work in progress."

"The sad guitar moved me."

"That's a self-portrait."

The garage was crowded with equipment, half the cables labeled and the other half apparently living by instinct. A blue light on the cassette recorder blinked at us. Outside, a delivery truck went past, rattling the window hard enough to shake a loose pencil off the shelf.

We'd agreed to spend the afternoon working on something new. I hadn't understood how difficult new could be for somebody whose older songs still carried so much of his life.

Greg tested a chord, stopped, and started it again.

"Does it sound too much like something I used to play?" he asked.

"Which something?"

He didn't answer right away.

I sat on the floor beside the mixing desk. "You can say Rose's name."

"I know. Sometimes I worry that if I bring her into a room, you won't have enough space left in it."

"That's a pretty crowded room you've imagined."

He rubbed the back of his neck. "Yeah."

I reached for the notebook, then stopped. "Can I write an idea down?"

"Please. Save me from the guitar face."

I wrote a sentence about a road that changed under the wheels without pretending the places behind us hadn't been real. It wasn't a lyric yet. It was something we could disagree about.

Greg read it. "That feels too neat."

"How?"

"Roads don't always take you someplace better. Sometimes you just take a different turn."

"Then write that."

He picked up the pencil. Half a minute later he was laughing.

"Great. I made it depressing."

"You made it true."

We worked for an hour and produced a spectacularly bad bridge, which wasn't a good sign for a song or the people singing it. Greg played one version with so much enthusiasm that a loose speaker vibrated off its stand. I caught the cable before it dragged the recorder with it.

"That's it," I said. "The equipment is voting no."

Greg looked mournfully at the stand. "Critics."

We took a break to repair it. He showed me how to wrap a cable properly rather than letting me pretend I knew. I was grateful he didn't turn the lesson into a demonstration of how talented he was; he made mistakes, too, and admitted when he'd mislabeled a channel.

As he retightened a knob, he said, "I used to think the way to prove I meant something was to turn every feeling into a song."

"And now?"

"Now I'm trying to work out whether I can just tell you stuff."

"You can."

"Okay." He set the screwdriver down. "I miss her. Sometimes I miss the version of me who didn't know how complicated everything would get. And I really, really like being here with you."

I felt my chest tighten.

"Thank you for telling me."

"That's it?"

"Did you want a drum solo?"

He laughed. Then he looked at me with genuine uncertainty.

I moved closer. "I've told you I prefer polyamory, that I'm ethically non-monogamous. I love different people in different ways. It doesn't mean I want each relationship to prove it can replace the others. I don't want you to erase Rose to make room for me. And I don't need to erase the people I care about when I'm with you."

He took a breath. "So I can write a song that isn't a competition."

"Please. Competition songs sound exhausting."

We went back to the second verse. It was rougher now, less clever. He played it once, stopped, and revised two notes. When he let me hear the full song again, the new part didn't explain the old one away. It let the melody move forward.

We had to finish packing the instruments before dinner. Someone was borrowing the room the next morning, and there was a real schedule to honor. I labeled the last cable and watched Greg put the notebook into the case instead of leaving it where the damp could curl its pages.

At the door, he stopped.

"Could I kiss you before we leave?" he asked.

"Yes."

The kiss was a little clumsy because his guitar case was wedged between us. He put it down. I pulled him close, laughing when he nearly tripped over the strap. For a moment the garage smelled only of dust, warm electronics, and him.

He shut off the recording light.

We didn't finish the arrangement that night. We did finish talking. When I came back the following week, the notebook was still open to the second verse, and Greg had penciled one extra word in the margin: *again*.
